analysis.one_liner: Replaces federal income taxes with a 20% flat tax on wages and business income, exempting investment income.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or vote: it sat in the House Ways and Means Committee from November 1997 until the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have scrapped the current graduated income tax for individuals and corporations. Individuals would pay a single 20% rate, but only on money they earn from work — income from investments like capital gains, dividends, and interest would be taxed at 0%. Businesses would pay 20% on business income, but could deduct the full cost of equipment, property, and wages. The bill also raised the standard deduction substantially and cut the mortgage interest deduction cap from $1 million to $100,000.
analysis.who_benefits: Wealthy households living on investment income would pay nothing on capital gains, dividends, or interest, and businesses would get immediate expensing of equipment and property costs plus a lower effective rate than the then-current corporate rates. Workers with large families would benefit from the much larger standard deduction ($16,500 for joint filers, plus $4,500 per dependent, adjusted for inflation) [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: The bill sets a single 20% rate on individual taxable earned income, replacing the current multi-bracket structure, and defines taxable earned income as income from work only [S2][S3].
It raises the basic standard deduction to $16,500 for joint returns, $14,000 for heads of household, and $9,500 for singles, plus an additional $4,50 per dependent with inflation indexing [S3].

Businesses would pay 20% of business taxable income, with deductions for the full cost of inputs, employee compensation, and tangible and real property, plus carryover of excess deductions with interest [S3].
It replaces the existing corporate income tax with a tax on every person engaged in a business activity, whether an individual, partnership, or corporation [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: The tax burden would shift onto wages: because investment income for individuals is entirely excluded, households with salaries and wages carry the 20% rate while those living off capital pay nothing at the individual level. Homeowners with mortgages above the new $100,000 acquisition-debt cap (or $50,000 for home equity) would lose part of a deduction they have today [S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill taxes only 'earned income' for individuals, so capital gains, dividends, and interest would be untaxed at the individual level, meaning two people with identical total income could owe very different taxes depending on whether their money comes from work or investments [S3].

It cuts the home mortgage interest deduction cap from $1,000,000 of acquisition indebtedness (and $500,000 of other qualified debt) to $100,000 and $50,000, raising taxes on homeowners with larger mortgages, including existing ones, starting with tax years after 1997 [S2][S3].

The 20% flat rate with a larger standard deduction is a major restructuring of the entire federal income tax with no revenue scoring in the bill itself, so the fiscal effects on funding for government programs cannot be assessed from the bill text [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The design gives its largest benefit to the top of the income distribution: a 0% rate on all investment income and a business tax with full expensing, while the rate on work income stays at 20% and some homeowners lose deductions. The bigger standard deduction genuinely helps working families with children, but the bill's central feature is moving the tax base away from wealth and onto wages.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it died there when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999 [S5][S1].

narrative.text: Rep. Mark Souder introduced the bill on November 8, 1997, with Rep. Solomon, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day [S1][S5].
The bill attracted only two cosponsors, one Republican and one Democrat [S4].
The action history shows no hearings, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action after the referral [S5].
The 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999, and the bill was not enacted [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nothing changed, so the existing graduated income tax stayed in place, including the tax on investment income and the $1 million mortgage interest cap. Wage earners whose tax situation would have worsened under a wage-only 20% base, and homeowners with large mortgages, are better off because the bill died. The wealthiest households and businesses lost an opportunity for large tax cuts.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The current tax code stayed in place

against.name: House Committee on Ways and Means
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on November 8, 1997 and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was nominally bipartisan but tiny — one Republican and one Democrat cosponsor alongside the Republican sponsor — and no votes were ever taken, so no party positions are recorded.

industries.industry: Wealthy investors and capital income earners
industries.note: The bill exempts all individual investment income — capital gains, dividends, and interest — from tax, while keeping a 20% rate on wages. The benefit flows to households with large investment portfolios at the expense of the wage-based tax base that funds the government.

The bill replaces the corporate income tax with a 20% tax on business taxable income after full deduction of equipment, property, and wage costs — a substantially lower effective burden for many firms, with the cost shifted to the broader tax base.

industries.industry: Mortgage lenders and homebuyers with large mortgages
industries.note: The bill shrinks the mortgage interest deduction cap from $1 million of acquisition debt to $100,000, reducing the tax benefit of large mortgages and potentially the appeal of borrowing heavily for housing.
